November, nineteen twenty-two. Egypt's Valley of the Kings. A British archaeologist named Howard Carter has been digging for years and finding almost nothing. Then his team uncovers a step. Then another. Then a sealed door.
Carter makes a small hole, holds up a candle, and peers inside. Someone behind him asks, can you see anything? And he answers... yes. Wonderful things.
It was the tomb of Tootahnkahmoon. Almost untouched. More than five thousand objects. Gold, chariots, jewelry, the famous golden mask. And lying among all that treasure... two trumpets.
One is made of silver. The other is bronze or copper. Each one is a little longer than your arm from elbow to fingertip, and each came with a wooden core, slid inside to protect its shape.
The silver one is engraved with the names of the king, and with gods. Ahmoon, Rah, and Ptah.

These weren't party instruments. In Egyptian wall paintings, trumpets like these usually show up with soldiers. They were signals. A sharp, loud blast that told an army when to move. Instruments of war.
Fast forward to nineteen thirty-nine. The BBC wants to do something nobody has ever done. Play the pharaoh's trumpets live, on radio, to the whole world.
It takes months to get permission from the museum in Cairo. The presenter, Rex Keating, picks a British army bandsman named James Tappern to play them.

And then, according to Keating, things start going wrong. During rehearsal, the silver trumpet shatters, and has to be repaired. On his way to the broadcast, his car is hit by a runaway horse and carriage. And just before they go live, the power in the museum goes out. So they play it by candlelight.
On the sixteenth of April, nineteen thirty-nine, a sound that had been silent for over three thousand years goes out across the airwaves.
After the broadcast, letters pour in from around the world. And many of them say the same thing. These are war trumpets. By playing them to the world, you have released the curse of war.
On the first of September, nineteen thirty-nine, Germany invades Poland. The Second World War begins. It will become the deadliest war in human history.

And the story doesn't end there. Years later, the curator of the Tootahnkahmoon collection at the Egyptian Museum, Hahla Hassahn, said the trumpet has magical powers. Whenever someone blows into it, she said, a war occurs.
She pointed to nineteen sixty-seven, when the trumpet was played, and the Six Day War followed. And to nineteen ninety-one, and the Gulf War.
And then, in two thousand and eleven, a museum staff member blew into the trumpet while it was being photographed. One week later, Egypt's revolution broke out.
And it gets weirder. On the twenty-eighth of January, two thousand and eleven, in the middle of that revolution, thieves broke into the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
When the staff checked the Tootahnkahmoon collection, one thing was missing. The bronze trumpet. Gone.
Weeks later, it turned up. Not in a vault. Not on the black market. It was found in a bag, at a station on the Cairo Metro, along with other stolen treasures. Nobody really knows how it got there.

So. Is it really cursed? Let's be honest. When the trumpets were played in April nineteen thirty-nine, Europe was already sliding toward war. Germany had taken over Czechoslovakia the month before. The war was coming, trumpet or no trumpet.
And the twentieth century had wars almost every single year. Pick any date, and you'll find one close by.

Egyptologists say there's no curse at all. But here's the part I love. These were made to announce war. Three thousand years later, that's still the story people tell about them. Maybe the trumpets are just doing their job.

So, what do they sound like? We're not going to play the real one. Just in case. This is our own take, a tribute. A short, bright horn, played on just a few notes, in rhythm, the way an ancient army signal might have sounded. Turn it up... and listen.
Two trumpets. Three thousand years of silence. One radio broadcast. And a legend that just won't die.
